edits.english: The Gemara references the Mishnaic discussion (Horayot 3b:12) where ben Azzai said to Rabbi Akiva: In what way is this person who went overseas different from one who sits in his house? The Gemara asks: Rabbi Akiva said well to ben Azzai. How did a scholar of ben Azzai's caliber fail to understand that distinction?

We learned in the Mishna: Ben Azzai said to him: In what way is this different from one who sits in his house? And Rabbi Akiva answered him that one who goes overseas has no possibility to hear. And they ask: Rabbi Akiva said well to ben Azzai in explaining the difference, and how did a great sage like ben Azzai not understand this?

And this answer is so simple, that it is puzzling that ben Azzai would ask a question whose answer is clear. And for this reason, Rava explains that ben Azzai surely did not come to ask about one who is already overseas, but rather he understood from Rabbi Akiva's words that the expression "went overseas" means one who is about to go there, who is on his way there and is not yet there.
Set out on the way - to go overseas, but he is still in the city.

There is a practical difference between them - According to Rabbi Akiva, he is exempt, as he set out on the way. Since he is preoccupied, it would not have been possible for him to hear that they (the court) reversed their ruling. Therefore, he relies on the court and is completely exempt.

Rava said: Here we are not talking about one who has already gone overseas, but rather one who set out on the way, who has not yet left overseas, but is preoccupied with preparations for departure. And in this matter there is a practical difference between them. According to ben Azzai, he is liable — as he is in his home and there is no difference between him and one who sits in his home. According to Rabbi Akiva, he is exempt — as he has set out on the way and is considered as one who has left.

Because he is preoccupied with preparations for his journey, he does not hear the new developments each day. And some have asked: If it is due to preoccupation, why specifically for one going overseas? Why do we not also worry about one going to another city? And it was answered in one way that there is a distinction between the preoccupation of a short journey and that of a long journey. And furthermore, it can be said that what is stated as 'overseas' is not literal, but rather refers to anyone embarking on a long journey who is preoccupied with his affairs, and therefore does not know what is new (Magen Giborim).

One who was about to embark to countries overseas and performed a transgression on the basis of the ruling of the court that circulated throughout a majority of the public, even if he did so after the court reversed its ruling, is exempt from bringing an individual sin-offering, in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Akiva (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:5).
